issues.legal_issue: A custodian authority empowered to administer evacuee property has jurisdiction to cancel an allotment of that property.
material_facts: The allottees received quasi-permanent allotments of evacuee land.
Their allotments were cancelled after it was found that their claims concerned lower-grade land than the land allotted to them.
The cancellation was made by the Deputy Custodian.
issues.conclusion: The Deputy Custodian had jurisdiction to cancel the allotments under both the applicable state legislation and its successor central legislation.
issues.legal_principle: The definition of “allotment” in section 2(a), the custodian’s cancellation power under section 12(1), and the rule-making power under section 56(2)(h) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, corresponded in substance to the relevant provisions of the East Punjab Evacuees’ (Administration of Property) Act, 1947. Those provisions conferred authority to cancel allotments. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.evacuee_property_allotment_cancellation_: The proceeding challenges the cancellation of an allotment of evacuee property.
predicates.cancellation_made_by_empowered_custodian: An officer empowered to administer the evacuee property made the cancellation.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges cancellation of an evacuee-property allotment and an empowered custodian made the cancellation, the cancellation is within that officer’s jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: Cancellation of an evacuee-property allotment is not invalid for lack of notice where the governing rules do not require notice for allotment cancellations and the allottee has an opportunity to present their case.
material_facts: The rules required notice and an opportunity to be heard before cancellation or variation of a lease, but did not provide for notice before cancellation of an allotment.
The allottees received notice to show cause, appeared before the Assistant Custodian, and had their statements recorded before the Deputy Custodian cancelled their allotments.
The Assistant Custodian acted under the Deputy Custodian’s orders and reported after hearing the allottees.
issues.conclusion: The cancellation was not without jurisdiction or invalid for want of notice or a hearing; the allottees had an opportunity to present their case, and the rules did not require notice for cancellation of an allotment.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 14(4) required notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard for cancellation or variation of a lease, but the rules made under section 56 did not impose that requirement for cancellation of an allotment. The Court also held that the allottees had in fact been heard, so there was no merit in the objection that the Deputy Custodian had not personally heard them again. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.evacuee_property_allotment_cancellation_: The proceeding challenges cancellation of an allotment of evacuee property.
predicates.rules_do_not_require_notice_for_allotmen: The applicable rules require notice for lease cancellation but do not require it for cancellation of an allotment.
predicates.allottee_received_opportunity_to_be_hear: The allottee received notice and an opportunity to present their case before the cancellation was made.

issues.definition: If an evacuee-property allotment is cancelled under rules that do not require notice for that kind of cancellation, and the allottee had an opportunity to be heard, the cancellation is not invalid for lack of notice or a hearing.

issues.legal_issue: Interim governmental instructions that are not given statutory force do not undo an already effective cancellation of an allotment.
material_facts: The allotments were cancelled before the later governmental letter concerning implementation of cancellation orders.
The letter set out an interim policy pending amendment of the rules, but no rule was made to give that policy statutory force.
The allottees relied on the letter to argue that their allotments should not be treated as cancelled.
issues.conclusion: The interim instructions did not nullify the cancellation or restore the allottees’ lost right to possession, and the challenged orders remained valid.
issues.legal_principle: A policy statement or interim instruction pending amendment of rules does not acquire statutory force without a rule giving effect to it. Once a valid cancellation order has been made, a later direction about implementation does not restore the right to possession already lost. Even if the letter were treated as a direction under section 54 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, it could not restore that lost right. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.evacuee_property_allotment_cancellation_: The proceeding concerns the effect of instructions on cancellation of an evacuee-property allotment.
predicates.cancellation_order_already_made: The authority made the cancellation order before the later instruction was issued.
predicates.later_instruction_not_given_statutory_fo: The later instruction was not implemented through a rule giving it statutory force.

issues.definition: When a cancellation order has already been made and a later instruction is not given statutory force, the instruction does not restore the cancelled allotment.

issues.legal_issue: Cancellation of a quasi-permanent evacuee-property allotment under lawful authority does not, in these circumstances, establish a breach of the allottee’s constitutional property right.
material_facts: The allottees held land under a quasi-permanent settlement that did not confer proprietary rights or permanent rights of occupation.
The allotments were subject to the evacuee-property legislation and were cancelled by an authority with jurisdiction after the allottees had an opportunity to present their case.
The allottees challenged the cancellation as a deprivation of their constitutional property right.
issues.conclusion: The allottees did not establish a breach of a fundamental right, and the challenged orders were valid and within jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: The quasi-permanent character of the settlement did not make an allotment irrevocable: the land remained subject to the governing evacuee-property legislation and the custodian’s cancellation powers. Because the cancellation was within jurisdiction and the allottees had been heard, the Court found no breach of the property right asserted under article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.constitutional_property_right_challenge: The proceeding claims that cancellation of an allotment breached a constitutional property right.
predicates.quasi_permanent_allotment_subject_to_can: The allotment was quasi-permanent and remained subject to the governing authority’s power to cancel it.
predicates.lawful_cancellation_after_opportunity_to: An empowered authority lawfully cancelled the allotment after the allottee had an opportunity to present their case.

issues.definition: A constitutional property-right challenge does not establish a breach when a quasi-permanent allotment remained subject to cancellation and an empowered authority lawfully cancelled it after giving the allottee an opportunity to be heard.
